summary: This memo presents the set of protocols and procedures that make up Inter-Domain Policy Routing, which lets routes between networks follow policies. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: IDPR is a set of protocols for inter-domain policy routing, where the route a packet takes is chosen by rules the network owners set rather than by distance alone. It covers who may carry which traffic, what quality and price they offer, and how a path is built and torn down when a link fails.

subtitle: A 1993 protocol suite that lets routes between networks follow the policies their owners set.

tldr.problem: Internet routing picked paths by shortest distance, so a network operator could not express rules such as which partners to favour, which traffic to refuse, or what quality and price a transit should offer.
tldr.mechanism: IDPR defines a set of protocols: policy gateways flood transit policies and connectivity to route servers, route servers generate policy routes from those policies, path agents set up paths along the chosen routes, and data messages travel under a path identifier.
tldr.outcome: The RFC specifies the whole suite, from the message formats to path setup and repair. The RFC Editor index lists its status as Historic, and no later RFC obsoletes it.

facts.label: IP protocol numbers
facts.value: 35 for data messages, 38 for control messages

facts.label: Data message header fields
facts.value: VERSION, PROTO, LENGTH, PATH ID, TIMESTAMP and INT/AUTH

today: RFC 1479 is a July 1993 standards-track memo that the RFC Editor index lists as Historic. No later RFC obsoletes it, so it is kept here as a record of the IDPR protocol suite.

sections.title: What IDPR Sets Out to Do
sections.content:
IDPR is the set of protocols and procedures that make up Inter-Domain Policy Routing. Its objective is to construct and maintain routes between source and destination administrative domains that provide user traffic with the services requested, within the constraints stipulated for the domains transited. It supports link state routing information distribution and route generation in conjunction with source specified message forwarding. The architecture is designed to accommodate an internetwork with tens of thousands of administrative domains collectively containing hundreds of thousands of local networks, and the details inside a domain, such as the gateways, networks and links a route traverses, are left to that domain's own routing.

IDPR performs five functions. It collects and distributes routing information, including domain transit policies and inter-domain connectivity. It generates and selects policy routes based on that information and on the source policies configured or requested. It sets up paths across the Internet using the policy routes generated. It forwards messages across and between domains along the established paths. And it maintains databases of routing information, inter-domain policy routes, forwarding information and configuration information.

Several entities share out the work. Policy gateways, the only IDPR-recognized connecting points between adjacent domains, collect and distribute routing information, take part in path setup, forward data messages along established paths, and maintain forwarding information databases. Path agents, resident within policy gateways and within route servers, act on behalf of hosts to select policy routes, set up and manage paths and maintain forwarding information databases, so any Internet host can benefit as long as a path agent is configured to act for it. A path agent in one domain may act on behalf of hosts in another, in which case the path agent's domain is an IDPR proxy for the hosts' domain.

Route servers maintain both the routing information database and the route database, and generate policy routes using the routing information collected and the source policies requested by path agents. A route server may reside within a policy gateway, or exist as an autonomous entity, and separating the route server functions frees the policy gateways from both the memory intensive work of database maintenance and the computationally intensive work of route generation. Mapping servers maintain the database of mappings that resolve Internet names and addresses to domain identifiers, and that function is to be integrated into the existing DNS name service. Configuration servers maintain the databases of configured information that apply to IDPR entities within their domains, including transit policies, source policies and mappings between local IDPR entities and their names and addresses, and are to be integrated into the domain's existing network management system.
sections.plainLanguage: IDPR aims at one thing: let the people who run networks decide which routes their traffic takes. Each network publishes what it offers and what it refuses, a route server works out a path that satisfies both ends, and the traffic is then sent along that path.

sections.title: Administrative Domains, Virtual Gateways and Policy Gateways
sections.content:
An administrative domain is a collection of contiguous hosts, gateways, networks and links managed by a single administrative authority. The domain administrator defines service restrictions for transit traffic and service requirements for locally generated traffic, and selects the addressing schemes and routing procedures that apply within the domain. Within the Internet, each domain has a unique numeric identifier assigned by IANA.

Virtual gateways are the only IDPR-recognized connecting points between adjacent domains. Each virtual gateway is a collection of directly-connected policy gateways in two adjoining domains, whose existence has been sanctioned by the administrators of both domains, and the two administrators may agree to establish more than one virtual gateway between the same two domains. For each one, the two administrators together assign a local numeric identifier, unique within the set of virtual gateways connecting the two domains, and a domain administrator concatenates that local identifier with the adjacent domain's identifier to produce an identifier unique within its own domain.

Policy gateways are the physical gateways within a virtual gateway. Each one enforces the service restrictions on IDPR transit traffic stipulated by the domain administrator and forwards the traffic accordingly. Within a domain, two policy gateways are neighbors if they are in different virtual gateways, and a single policy gateway may belong to several virtual gateways. Within a virtual gateway, two policy gateways are peers if they are in the same domain and adjacent if they are in different domains. Adjacent policy gateways are directly connected if the only Internet-addressable entities attached to the connecting medium are policy gateways in the virtual gateways, which means that a network can serve as a direct connection and not only a point-to-point link.

A domain component is a subset of a domain's entities such that all entities within the subset are mutually reachable via intra-domain routes, but no entities outside the subset are reachable from entities within it. A domain normally consists of a single component, namely itself, but when partitioned it consists of several components. Each component has an identifier unique within the Internet, composed of the domain identifier together with the identifier of the lowest-numbered operational policy gateway within the component, and all operational policy gateways in a component can determine that lowest number consistently through intra-domain routing information, without explicit negotiation.
sections.plainLanguage: The building blocks are the administrative domain, which is one organisation's part of the network, and the virtual gateway, an agreed crossing point between two domains. Each crossing point is made of real gateways, one on each side, called policy gateways.

sections.title: Source and Transit Policies
sections.content:
Each domain administrator sets transit policies that dictate how and by whom the resources in its domain may be used. Transit policies are usually public, and they specify offered services comprising access restrictions, such as those applied to traffic to or from certain domains or classes of users; quality, such as delay, throughput or error characteristics; and monetary cost, such as a charge per byte, message or unit of time.

Each domain administrator also sets source policies for traffic originating in its domain. Source policies are usually private, and they specify requested services comprising access restrictions, such as domains to favor or avoid in routes; quality, such as acceptable delay, throughput and reliability; and monetary cost, such as acceptable session cost.

A source policy takes the form of a collection of sets. It names the groups of source and destination traffic flows it applies to, the transit domains those flows should favor, avoid or exclude, the source user class, and the requested services that are not access restrictions. The path agent must honour the policy when it selects a route: no domain marked as excluded may appear in the route, and the route must provide the services listed as requested.

A transit policy also takes the form of a collection of sets. It names the source and destination hosts and domains it applies to, the temporal access restrictions, meaning the time intervals during which the policy applies, the user class access restrictions, the offered services that are not access restrictions, and the virtual gateway access restrictions, which are the domain entry and exit points the policy applies to. A domain advertising such a transit policy will carry traffic from any host in the listed source set to any host in the listed destination set, provided that the traffic enters the domain during one of the listed intervals, carries one of the listed user class identifiers, enters through a virtual gateway listed as an entry point and leaves through one listed as an exit point.
sections.plainLanguage: Each network writes two kinds of rules. A transit policy says what the network is willing to carry for others, and is usually public. A source policy says what the network's own traffic wants, and is usually private. A route has to satisfy both.

sections.title: How IDPR Messages Travel
sections.content:
There are two kinds of IDPR messages: data messages containing user data generated by hosts, and control messages containing protocol-related control information generated by policy gateways and route servers. Within an internetwork, only policy gateways and route servers are able to generate, recognize and process IDPR messages, and the existence of IDPR is invisible to all other gateways and hosts.

The RFC considered embedding IDPR in IP as a set of IP options and rejected the idea, because only domains that support IP would be able to participate, because every gateway in a participating domain would at least have to recognize the IDPR option even if it did not execute the IDPR protocols, and because the size restrictions on IP options would preclude the inclusion of all the necessary information for some protocols, in particular path control. It therefore uses encapsulation. An IDPR message tunnels from source to destination across an internetwork through domains that may employ disparate intra-domain addressing schemes and routing procedures, and each policy gateway encapsulates the message with, for example, an IP header that will enable it to reach the next policy gateway, and indicates in the protocol field of the encapsulating header that the message is an IDPR message. Only the recipient policy gateway interprets the protocol field, strips off the encapsulating header and processes the message. That gateway should verify that the source and destination addresses in the encapsulating header match the adjacent policy gateway's address and its own, and that the message arrived on the interface designated for the direct connection. When encapsulated within IP messages, IDPR data messages carry the IP protocol number 35 and IDPR control messages carry 38, so the two are told apart at the encapsulating protocol level.

The path agent at a source domain prepends a header to each data message it selects for IDPR handling. The header holds a VERSION field, currently equal to 1; a PROTO field naming the protocol used to process the contents, which only the path agent at the destination interprets; a LENGTH field giving the length of the entire message in bytes; a 64-bit PATH ID assigned by the source's path agent; a 32-bit TIMESTAMP counting seconds since 1 January 1970 0:00 GMT; and a variable INT/AUTH field holding a computed integrity and authentication value.

Every IDPR message carries a single integrity and authentication value, which may be used not only to detect message corruption but also to verify the authenticity of the message source. The IANA sanctions the set of valid algorithms, which may include algorithms that only check message integrity, such as n-bit cyclic redundancy checks, as well as algorithms that also authenticate the source, such as signed hash functions of the message contents. Each control message must carry a non-null value, and the RFC recommends that control message integrity be based on a digital signature algorithm applied to a one-way hash function, such as RSA applied to MD5, which simultaneously verifies integrity and source authenticity. Data messages are not required to carry a non-null value, and the RFC recommends that a higher layer procedure, rather than IDPR, check the integrity and authenticity of data messages, because of the computation involved.

Each message also carries a timestamp supplied by the source entity, which indicates the age of the message. IDPR entities use the absolute value to confirm that a message is current, and the difference between two timestamps to decide which holds the more recent information. All IDPR entities must possess internal clocks that are synchronized to some degree, but the granularity required is on the order of minutes and can be achieved manually, so a clock synchronization protocol operating among all entities in all domains is useful but not necessary. Timestamp checks are required for control messages and are discretionary for data messages.
sections.plainLanguage: IDPR messages are wrapped in the addressing of each domain they cross, so one message can pass through networks that do not share an address scheme. Each message carries a path number, a timestamp and a value that lets the receiver check that the message was not altered and came from where it claims.

sections.title: How Routing Information Is Distributed
sections.content:
An AD representative policy gateway uses unrestricted flooding among all domains to distribute its domain's routing information messages to route servers. There are two kinds of routing information message issued by each AD representative. A CONFIGURATION message contains the transit policy information configured by the domain administrator, including for each transit policy its identifier, its specification, and the sets of virtual gateways configured as mutually reachable via intra-domain routes supporting the given transit policy. A DYNAMIC message contains information about current virtual gateway connectivity to adjacent domains, and about the sets of virtual gateways currently mutually reachable via intra-domain routes supporting the configured transit policies.

After generating a routing information message, the AD representative distributes a copy to each of its peers and to a selected VG representative in all other virtual gateways connected to the domain, and each VG representative in turn distributes a copy to each of its peers. Each routing information message carries a sequence number which, together with the timestamp carried in the CMTP message header, determines the recency of the message. The AD representative sets the sequence number to 0 if its internal clock time is greater than the timestamp in its previously generated message, and to one greater than the previous sequence number if the clock time is equal. The sequence number may look superfluous, because multiple distinct messages with identical timestamps are not expected, but it becomes necessary when the internal clock of an AD representative is synchronized, since the clock value may have to be frozen during that interval.

Route servers maintain both the routing information database and the route database, and answer requests for information from policy gateways and other route servers. Those requests and responses are the messages exchanged by the Route Server Query Protocol. A requesting entity always queries local route servers before remote ones, to contain the cost of the query and the response, because a remote request needs a policy route and an established path before the two can talk.

A request is acceptable if it passes the CMTP validation checks and its timestamp is less than rsqp_old, 300 seconds, behind the recipient's internal clock. A route server may fail to fill a request because its database holds no entry or only a partial entry for the requested information, or because special message distribution rules imposed by the domain administrator preclude releasing it, and it then responds with a negative acknowledgement. If the requesting entity receives a negative acknowledgement, or no acknowledgement after rsqp_ret attempts at the same route server, it queries a different route server, proceeding in round-robin order through its list, as long as the number of attempts does not exceed rsqp_try, 3. If it is still unsuccessful, it abandons the request and logs the event for network management.
sections.plainLanguage: Each network pushes two kinds of information to everyone: the rules it has configured, and what is reachable right now. When a gateway needs a route, it asks a route server, and tries the closest route server first.

sections.title: Path Setup and Data Forwarding
sections.content:
Two entities in different domains may exchange IDPR data messages only if there exists an IDPR path set up between the two domains. Path setup requires cooperation among path agents and intermediate policy gateways. Path agents locate policy routes, initiate the Path Control Protocol and manage existing paths between administrative domains, while intermediate policy gateways verify that a given policy route is consistent with their domain's transit policies, establish the forwarding information, and forward messages along existing paths. The path agent that initiates path setup in the source domain is the originator, and the one that handles the originator's message in the destination domain is the target.

Once a path for a policy route is set up, its physical realization is a set of consecutive policy gateways, with policy gateways or route servers forming the endpoints, and two successive entities in the set belong to either the same domain or the same virtual gateway. A policy gateway or route server may at any time recover the resources dedicated to a path that goes through it by tearing that path down, for example when a path has not been used for some period of time. The Path Control Protocol may build multiple paths between source and destination domains, but it is not responsible for managing them as a group or for eliminating redundant paths.

The RFC works through an example. A host Hx in domain AD X wants to communicate with a host Hy in domain AD Y, and both domains support IDPR. Hx need not know the identity of its own domain or of Hy's domain. It simply forwards the message to one of the gateways on its local network, and eventually the message arrives at a policy gateway in AD X, since policy gateways are the only egress points to other domains. The path agent resident in that gateway uses the message header, including source and destination addresses and any requested service information, to decide whether the message is intra-domain or inter-domain and whether it needs an IDPR policy route, by looking for a forwarding information database entry for the traffic flow. A radix search is recommended.

If no entry exists for a new IDPR traffic flow, the path agent first determines the source and destination domains associated with the message's addresses, relying on the mapping servers and caching their responses locally, and then attempts to obtain a policy route, relying on the route servers and caching their responses in the same way. The route server consults its route database and, if it cannot locate a suitable route, attempts to generate at least one route to the destination domain that is consistent with the requested services. It always returns a response, and the response to a successful query is a set of candidate routes from which the path agent makes its selection. A path agent will normally choose a single route, though IDPR does not preclude choosing several, for example to support fault tolerance or load balancing.

For a new route there is no existing path, so the path agent sets one up. It associates an identifier with the path, which is included in each message that travels down the path and is used by the policy gateways along the path to determine how to forward the message. It then initiates path setup, communicating the policy route, in terms of requested services, constituent domains, relevant transit policies and connecting virtual gateways, to the policy gateways in intermediate domains. Each intermediate policy gateway determines whether to accept or refuse the path and to which next policy gateway to forward the path setup information, and the setup procedure allows policy gateways to set up a path in both directions simultaneously. After accepting, each intermediate policy gateway updates its forwarding information database to associate the path identifier with the appropriate previous and next hop policy gateways. When a policy gateway in AD Y accepts a path, it notifies the source path agent in AD X, and paths remain in place until they are torn down because of failure, expiration, or when resources are scarce.

Each path has an identifier unique throughout an internetwork, made up of the identifier of the originator's domain, the identifier of the originator's policy gateway or route server, and a 32-bit local path identifier specified by the originator. The local path identifier must differ from that of any other active or recently torn-down path originally set up by that path agent, which helps to distinguish new paths from replays, and the originator must keep a record of each extinct path for long enough that all policy gateways on it have dropped their references to it.
sections.plainLanguage: Before traffic can cross, a path has to be built. The path agent finds a route that fits the policies, asks each gateway along the way to join in, and gets a number for the path. Every later message carries that number, so each gateway knows where to send it next.

items.title: Collect and distribute
items.text: Gather domain transit policies and inter-domain connectivity, and spread them to the route servers.

items.title: Generate and select
items.text: Work out policy routes from that information and from the source policies requested.

items.title: Set up paths
items.text: Build the paths across the Internet that the chosen policy routes call for.

items.title: Forward messages
items.text: Carry messages across and between domains along the established paths.

items.title: Maintain databases
items.text: Keep the routing information, policy route, forwarding and configuration data.
